sources.text: UN Extends Mission to Take Down Gangs in Haiti. That’s why it’s so significant that the UN has undertaken a new approach. The United Nations–backed Gang Suppression Force which was authorized by UN Security Council Resolution 2793 in September 2025 has been reauthorized. It supports an international police and military mission in Haiti to combat armed gangs and restore public safety, working alongside the Haitian National Police and Armed Forces of Haiti. And the results are beginning to show, said Ambassador Waltz. The “Gang Suppression Force is taking the fight to the gangs. They’re clearing roads and neighborhoods. They’re liberating what has been no-go zones for the Haitian National Police. They are shutting down illegal tolls that serve as a revenue source for the gangs, an illicit revenue source, and keeps them fueled for their terror.” There are several things that make this model different, said Ambassador Waltz. First, it has enforcement power with soldiers who have an offensive mandate. The entire effort is designed around the ultimate objective that Haitians themselves take back control of their own security and their own future. That means this will not become an endless mission, declared Ambassador Waltz. And finally, countries are actually sharing the burden to staff and support this mission in Haiti. Over the last year, more than 17,000 personnel have been pledged to fill 5,500 authorized billets. There are now more than 1,500 troops on the ground in Haiti with 4,000 more slated to arrive in the coming months. But this is just the beginning, cautioned Ambassador Waltz. “There’s more work to do, and the gangs are certainly not just melting away, and their terror over the people of this region continues.” The United States believes the UN can deliver on missions like the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. The Haitian people have faced many hardships, including earthquakes and hurricanes. “Together. . .we can take back the second oldest republic in our hemisphere,” declared Ambassador Waltz. “They can win back their streets and their lives and their futures for their families.”

sources.title: Haiti Gang Crisis Explained 2026 Gangs and the UN Force
sources.excerpt: Haiti's gang crisis explained: who the gangs are, how they took Port-au-Prince, the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, and what it means for foreigners.
sources.text: Haiti Gang Crisis Explained 2026 Gangs and the UN Force. Haiti’s gang crisis explained for outsiders: who the armed groups are and how they captured the capital. It also covers the new international force and what the violence means for anyone with family, business or plans in the country. Haiti is a country where armed gangs, not the state, decide who can use the main roads out of the capital. A UN-backed force is trying to reverse that, while a caretaker government prepares the first national vote in a decade. Haiti occupies the western third of Hispaniola, a Caribbean island it shares with the Dominican Republic. About 11.9 million people lived there in 2025, according to the World Bank, and nearly all of them speak Haitian Creole. The crisis is a long armed takeover of the capital region by criminal groups. Gangs control up to 90 percent of Port-au-Prince, by UN estimates, and now reach deep into farmland. This is not a civil war between two political camps. It is a contest between heavily armed gangs, a weak national police force and a slowly arriving international mission. The currency is the gourde, which traded at about 130.6 gourdes per US dollar in late September 2026. That rate comes from the Banque de la République d’Haïti, the central bank. The current spiral began with the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in his home on 7 July 2021. Since then Haiti has had no elected president, and the terms of the last elected senators expired in 2023. In early 2024 the gangs launched a joint offensive on the capital. They broke open two major prisons and shut the international airport, stranding Prime Minister Ariel Henry abroad. Henry announced his resignation on 11 March 2024. A nine-member Transitional Presidential Council, sworn in on 25 April 2024, took over the presidency. That council dissolved on 7 February 2026 without a successor. Executive power passed to Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, in office since November 2024, who now governs alone. The Rio Times has followed the legal fallout of the 2021 killing too. In September 2026 Haiti sent 18 suspects in the Moïse case to the United States for trial. The dominant force is Viv Ansanm, Creole for “living together”, a coalition founded in September 2023. It joined the two rival gang federations of the capital, known as G9 and G-Pèp. Its best-known figure is Jimmy Chérizier, a former police officer nicknamed “Barbecue”. In August 2025 US prosecutors charged him with conspiring to violate sanctions, and Washington offers up to US$5 million for his arrest. Jeanine Pirro, a federal prosecutor in Washington, called him “a gang leader responsible for heinous human rights abuses”. As of September 2026 he has not been arrested, and the charges remain allegations untested in court. Outside the capital, the main armed group is Gran Grif, based in the Artibonite valley, Haiti’s main farming region. On 2 May 2025 the US State Department designated both Viv Ansanm and Gran Grif as foreign terrorist organisations. That designation has practical weight for outsiders. Paying a gang, even for safe passage, can now expose a company or donor to US terrorism-financing law. Gangs earn money mainly through kidnapping for ransom, extortion and robbery. The UN’s political office in Haiti, BINUH, recorded 81 kidnappings from April to June 2026, up from 57 in the first quarter. BINUH, the UN Integrated Office in Haiti, publishes the most detailed casualty counts. It recorded 1,642 people killed and 745 injured from January to March 2026. From April to June it counted 1,408 killed and 656 injured. Gang attacks caused about 55 percent of those casualties, and security-force operations over 40 percent. For comparison, the UN counted 5,601 people killed in gang violence across all of 2024. Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, said then that the figures could not capture “the absolute horrors being perpetrated in Haiti”. Sexual violence is used as a weapon of control. BINUH documented 796 victims in the second quarter of 2026, and 87 percent were raped by several attackers. Displacement has reached a record. The International Organization for Migration, the UN migration agency, said in June 2026 that nearly 1.5 million people had fled their homes. Hunger follows the violence. About 5.8 million Haitians, more than half the population, faced acute food insecurity in April 2026, the UN-backed IPC hunger monitor said. The violence is spreading well beyond the capital. In March 2026 a Gran Grif attack near Petite-Rivière killed at least 70 people, the Haitian rights group Defenseurs Plus said. Official counts for that attack were lower, at 16 to 17 dead, which shows how hard verification is. In August 2026 an attack killed at least 47 people in Kenscoff , a hillside town above the capital. The first outside answer was a Kenyan-led police mission, approved by the UN Security Council in October 2023. Its first 400 Kenyan officers landed in Port-au-Prince on 25 June 2024. That mission never had enough people or money. It peaked at roughly 1,000 personnel, and the International Crisis Group, a conflict think tank, called it largely a failure. On 30 September 2025 the Security Council replaced it with the Gang Suppression Force, or GSF, in Resolution 2793. The vote was 12 in favour, with China, Russia and Pakistan abstaining. The new force may have up to 5,550 uniformed personnel and, unlike its predecessor, can arrest suspected gang members. A new UN Support Office in Haiti supplies its food, medical care and transport. The first 400 Chadian troops arrived in April 2026. By July it had just over 1,000 personnel from six countries, including Chad, Jamaica and Sri Lanka, the Jamaica Observer reported. Al Jazeera reported about 1,500 deployed by late September, around 30 percent of the planned size. At the end of September 2026 the Council extended the mandate for six months, to 31 March 2027. sources.text: Haitian conflict. Since 2020, Haiti's capital Port-au-Prince has been the site of an ongoing armed conflict. The government of Haiti and Haitian security forces have struggled to maintain their control of Port-au-Prince amid this conflict, with gangs speculated to control up to 90% of the city by 2023. In response to the escalating fighting, an armed vigilante movement, known as bwa kale, also emerged, with the purpose of fighting the gangs. On 2 October 2023, United Nations Security Council Resolution 2699 was approved, authorizing a Kenya-led "multinational security support mission" to Haiti. Until 2024, the war was between two major groups and their allies: the Revolutionary Forces of the G9 Family and Allies and the G-Pèp. However, in February 2024 the two rival groups united in a coalition known as Viv Ansanm, formed to oppose the government and the UN mission.
